strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why adversarially trained networks can generalize on clean inputs while exhibiting poor robust generalization. Separating shared-feature learning from sample-specific noise memorization provides a concrete explanatory hypothesis.

The explicit patch distribution, cubic CNN, and signal/noise projections make the intended mechanism mathematically inspectable. Analyzing their evolution during optimization is well aligned with the paper’s objectives.

The MNIST and CIFAR-10 experiments examine input sensitivity across perturbation radii and training epochs. The observed differences between training and test loss geometry provide relevant exploratory evidence.
weaknesses: The main analysis does not establish low worst-case robust training error. GTA uses a fixed classifier based on the true signal direction, producing one signal-shrunk example per sample. Training error is measured on these examples, whereas robust test error maximizes over the entire perturbation ball. Fitting the prescribed examples does not establish robustness throughout training neighborhoods. Consequently, Theorem 4.1 does not demonstrate the standard robust generalization gap motivating the paper.

The proof of Theorem 4.1 contains consequential mathematical gaps. Appendix C.12 treats a cubic polynomial of Gaussian noise as sub-Gaussian, which is generally false, and infers that every noise-weight norm is Θ(1) from aggregate memorization quantities V_i = Θ(1), without establishing that implication. These steps underpin the test-error conclusions and require corrected concentration arguments and explicit control of the noise-weight norms.

The construction supporting Theorem 5.2 need not retain positive robust test error. Assumption 5.1 permits a distribution on two well-separated points with a nonrobust clean classifier. Once both points are sampled, construction (C) is robust throughout the distribution’s support. No coverage or probability-mass assumption excludes this case. Appendix D also claims uniform o(1) approximation of the generally discontinuous construction by continuous ReLU networks, which its smoothing argument does not establish.

Theorem 7.1 is invalid under its stated assumptions. A constant predictor has zero input-gradient flatness, yet unequal losses across labels produce empirical–population fluctuations, so population risk can exceed empirical risk with nonvanishing probability. The bound includes no residual sampling term. Appendix E also leaves KDE bias/variance terms and a radius-dependent flatness term without deriving the stated sample-size rate. Furthermore, Proposition 7.2 concerns the adversarial–clean population risk difference, which is a different quantity from a train–test generalization gap.

The experiments do not directly validate the proposed memorization mechanism. Local flattening and increasing test sensitivity are compatible with multiple explanations; neither establishes learning of sample-specific noise or convergence to construction (C). Direct feature measurements or interventions are absent, and the authors’ experiments do not report the clean/robust accuracy trajectories central to the motivating phenomenon. Attack settings, procedures for maximizing gradient norms, and repeated-run uncertainty are insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction.

The claimed extension of the representation lower bound beyond Li et al. (2022) is not substantively established. Theorem 5.3 remains existential, and Appendix D constructs linearly separable data, already within the earlier setting. Allowing neural-separable distributions therefore does not itself strengthen the result. Moreover, this worst-case existence argument does not establish an optimization preference for CGRO classifiers on typical data.
